A1.justification: Despite the changed title and terminology, both PDFs describe the same core research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable, allowing retained, relocated, added and removed content to be matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original retrieval experiments on four datasets, training and query-selection ablations, qualitative examples, and an additional video-to-text retrieval experiment.

after.justification: V2 retains original retrieval experiments and adds LLM-choice comparisons, additional query-selection ablations, and measured computational costs.

M1.justification: The core CLIP/X-Pool architecture, losses, KTS captioning, LLM prompt, FQS selection and voting remain unchanged. A limited method-level removal is v1 Appendix A.4's video-to-text adaptation, which generated captions as auxiliary queries for video inputs. V2's thresholded FQS and NQS variants are experimental alternatives, not replacements for the central method.

E1.justification: MSR-VTT, MSVD, LSMDC and VATEX remain, but v2 removes the entire additional video-to-text retrieval task evaluated on MSR-VTT in v1 Appendix A.4 and Table 10. This materially narrows task coverage by eliminating the reverse retrieval direction. The new LLM and timing experiments change configurations and procedures rather than adding another dataset or task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds ProST, UCOFIA, UMT, T-MASS, TeachCLIP, KDProR and DITS, while removing CAMoE and CLIP2Video. Comparator membership also expands in Tables 2–4, including newly reported Cap4Video comparisons on MSVD and VATEX. Appendix A.2 adds selection alternatives, including NQS and similarity-constrained FQS.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a latency/memory evaluation with one query, 100,000 candidate videos and precomputed video embeddings, excluding LLM generation time. It also adds GPT-4 versus 3.8B Phi-3.5 configurations and fixed-k selection experiments with similarity thresholds. Existing dataset splits and training schedules remain unchanged; Tables 2–3 cease reporting mean rank.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to LLM choice and noisy individual queries, compare FQS against neighbor selection, NQS and similarity-threshold variants, and measure computational costs (v2 Tables 8–10). Figure 9 adds training-caption examples. Conversely, the reverse-retrieval caption-selection analysis in v1 Appendix A.4 is removed.

E5.justification: V2 identifies the four already-present random-selection rows in Table 7 as results from four different seeds; this newly discloses their provenance rather than demonstrating additional runs. Appendix A.4 also specifies averaging timing measurements over 1,000 randomly generated examples. No confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Retained principal scores are unchanged, including v1 Tables 8–9 relocated to v2 Tables 11–12. V2 adds LLM, selection-variant and computational results, while deleting reverse-retrieval results and MSVD/VATEX mean-rank entries. For example, Table 8 reports FQS R@1 of 52.1 for GPT-4 and 51.5 for Phi-3.5: a 0.6-point gap, despite the prose stating 0.5.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A.4 adds symbolic computational-cost definitions and Equations 10–11, separating encoder, similarity and LLM costs and simplifying under single-query retrieval with precomputed video embeddings. The original method equations remain unchanged; no new retrieval guarantee or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: V2 elevates the existing oracle-query analysis into an explicit claimed contribution in the introduction and conclusion. The central claims about data-centric enrichment during training and retrieval, effective query selection, and strong performance on four benchmarks remain substantially the same.

C2.justification: V2 adds the interpretation that FQS and voting mitigate noise from a weaker LLM, and hypothesizes that long concatenated descriptions challenge the text encoder. It more explicitly identifies oracle selection as impractical, acknowledges unmeasured LLM generation costs, and adds hallucination and LLM computation to the limitations. These refine the existing mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 documents the additional selection variants and Phi-3.5 configuration, and clarifies the GPU description as NVIDIA A10 24G. Its reproducibility statement promises public code, data and pretrained models, while v1's assertion that oracle-selection code accompanies the supplementary material disappears. Neither change establishes actual resource availability from the supplied PDFs.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around information asymmetry and foundation models. V2 adds discussion of T-MASS, InternVid, HAVTR and CLIP language rewriting, and develops the comparison with UATVR. It also removes much of v1's earlier multimodal query-expansion literature, changing the research context beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, replacing GQE/information-imbalance terminology with unified text enrichment/information asymmetry. Method and ablation subsections are reorganized, appendices are reordered, and acknowledgement, ethics and reproducibility statements are added.

P2.justification: V2 simplifies Figure 1, updates Figure 2 and redraws Figure 3 as a stepwise FQS illustration. It adds Tables 8–10 and Figure 9, removes the reverse-retrieval table, and restructures comparison tables, including dropping mean-rank columns from Tables 2–3 and marking larger-backbone comparators in grey. Existing qualitative examples are retained and relocated within the new conference layout.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens validation through additional selection and LLM ablations, updated comparisons, and measured computational costs. The cost analysis improves transparency: selection takes 147.92 ms versus 242.45 ms with all queries, but exceeds the 103.01 ms baseline and excludes LLM generation. These are useful, bounded gains; full deployment cost remains unresolved, and removing the video-to-text study reduces supporting task coverage.
